subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: Madelung's deformity results from retarded growth of which structure?

options.A: The lower end of the radius
options.B: The upper end of the humerus
options.C: The olecranon process of the ulna

questions.explanation: Madelung's deformity is a dorsal subluxation (displacement) of the lower end of the ulna, caused by retarded growth of the lower end of the radius.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: In epidemiological studies, 'comparability' between study and control groups is best ensured by:

options.A: Choosing groups of very different ages and backgrounds to maximise contrast
options.B: Randomization or random allocation, or 'matching' for selected characteristics when random allocation is not possible (e.g. case-control/cohort studies)
options.C: Always excluding any consideration of age or sex
options.D: Comparability is not actually necessary for valid epidemiological conclusions

questions.explanation: Comparability ('like being compared with like') between study and control groups is best ensured by randomization or random allocation. Where this is not possible, such as in case-control or cohort studies, 'matching' for selected characteristics is used instead, and standardization can address a limited number of characteristics like age, sex, and parity.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Making Comparisons
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: To achieve full passive range of hip flexion, the knee must also be allowed to flex. Why?

options.A: It relaxes tension on the two-joint hamstring muscle group, which would otherwise restrict hip flexion
options.B: It reduces pain in the lumbar spine
options.C: It is required purely to stabilize the pelvis
options.D: Knee position has no real effect on hip flexion range

questions.explanation: The hamstrings cross both the hip and knee. Keeping the knee extended while flexing the hip stretches the hamstrings and limits how far the hip can flex; flexing the knee releases that tension, allowing full hip flexion range to be reached.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Combined Hip and Knee Motion
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: Orchidopexy for a palpable undescended testis is ideally performed at what age, to optimise fertility outcomes?

options.A: Immediately at birth
options.B: Between 6 and 12 months of age
options.C: Only after puberty
options.D: Age has no bearing on fertility outcomes

questions.explanation: Orchidopexy is ideally performed as a day-case procedure between 6 and 12 months of age. Bringing the testis into the scrotum (below core body temperature) at a young age optimises spermatogenesis and fertility outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Damage to the motor cortex on the LEFT side of the brain will typically produce movement weakness on which side of the body?

options.A: The left side (same side)
options.B: The right side (opposite side), because motor fibers cross to the other side below the head
options.C: Both sides equally
options.D: Neither side — motor cortex damage never affects limb movement

questions.explanation: Fibers from the motor cortex on one side of the brain cross to the opposite side of the body on their way down to the spinal cord. So damage to the left motor cortex produces weakness, loss of dexterity, or spastic paralysis on the right side of the body below the head.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Sensory and Motor Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Beta-blockers such as propranolol are particularly useful for which type of anxiety?

options.A: Generalised anxiety disorder as first-line, long-term therapy
options.B: Anticipatory anxiety (e.g. before public speaking or examinations)
options.C: Anxiety secondary to hypothyroidism only

questions.explanation: Beta-blockers like propranolol and atenolol are particularly useful in managing anticipatory anxiety (such as anxiety before going on stage or sitting an exam), by controlling the physical/autonomic symptoms of anxiety, though care is needed in patients with asthma, bradycardia, or heart block.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder, Treatment
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Which two limbic system structures are most strongly implicated in the formation of new memories?

options.A: The olfactory bulb and septal nuclei
options.B: The hippocampus and the amygdala
options.C: The cingulate gyrus and corpus callosum

questions.explanation: Among the limbic system structures (olfactory bulb, septal nuclei, hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus), the hippocampus and amygdala in particular play a key role in the formation of new memories — as dramatically illustrated by the case of patient H.M., whose bilateral removal of these structures left him unable to form new long-term memories.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Limbic System
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Isolated blunt liver or splenic injury in a haemodynamically stable child is generally best managed by:

options.A: Immediate laparotomy in every case
options.B: Non-operative management with observation
options.C: Immediate splenectomy regardless of severity

questions.explanation: Isolated liver or splenic injury in a stable child can usually be managed non-operatively, with laparotomy reserved for ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding; uncomplicated cases can often be discharged after 5-7 days with a period of restricted activity.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: 'Rusty' coloured sputum is classically associated with infection by which organism?

options.A: Pseudomonas
options.B: Pneumococcus
options.C: Haemophilus

questions.explanation: Rusty-coloured sputum is a classic finding associated with pneumococcal infection (typical lobar pneumonia), whereas dark green/brown sputum suggests Pseudomonas, and 'red-currant jelly' sputum suggests Klebsiella.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Sputum
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Which of these is a classic feature of a panic attack, as distinguished from generalised anxiety?

options.A: Gradual worsening of mild anxiety over several months
options.B: A sudden, discrete episode of severe anxiety, often beginning unexpectedly 'out of the blue' and lasting only a few minutes
options.C: Anxiety present continuously for years without any discrete episodes
options.D: Anxiety that only occurs during sleep

questions.explanation: Panic disorder is characterised by discrete episodes of acute, severe anxiety that begin suddenly, often 'out of the blue' with no apparent precipitant, and last for a few minutes — quite different from the more continuous, lower-grade anxiety of generalised anxiety disorder.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A patent processus vaginalis that allows peritoneal fluid (but no bowel) to track down into the scrotum results in:

options.A: An inguinal hernia
options.B: A hydrocoele
options.C: A varicocele

questions.explanation: When a patent processus vaginalis allows only peritoneal fluid (not bowel) to track into the scrotum, the result is a hydrocoele — typically a non-tender, transilluminating scrotal swelling, distinct from an inguinal hernia where bowel or other abdominal content is present.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Hydrocoeles
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, the 'underlying cause of death' is recorded in Part I, and is defined as:

options.A: The immediate mode of dying, such as 'heart failure' or 'asthenia'
options.B: The disease or injury that initiated the chain of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence that produced the fatal injury
options.C: Any condition present at death regardless of its role in causing it
options.D: Only conditions diagnosed after an autopsy

questions.explanation: The underlying cause of death is the disease or injury that initiated the train of morbid events leading directly to death, or the circumstances of the accident/violence producing the fatal injury — the certificate explicitly notes this does NOT mean the immediate mode of dying (e.g. 'heart failure' or 'asthenia' are not acceptable as the underlying cause).
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for the 'milk ejection' or 'let-down' reflex during breastfeeding?

options.A: Prolactin
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Progesterone

questions.explanation: Oxytocin is the major galactokinetic hormone: suckling triggers a neural reflex arc to the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts, forcing milk down into the lactiferous ducts (the 'let-down' reflex). Prolactin, by contrast, drives milk secretion itself (lactogenesis/galactopoiesis), not its ejection.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Galactokinesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Pleuritic chest pain is best described as:

options.A: A dull, central, band-like pain radiating to the jaw
options.B: A severe, sharp, stabbing pain, worse on inspiration, and not reproduced by palpation
options.C: A burning retrosternal pain worse when lying flat or bending forward
options.D: Pain that is only ever felt during exercise and never at rest

questions.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, from inflammation of the parietal pleura, is classically a severe, sharp, stabbing pain that worsens on inspiration and is NOT reproduced by palpation — distinguishing it from musculoskeletal chest wall pain, which IS reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Massive haemoglobin absorption by the renal tubules in severe falciparum malaria produces which complication?

options.A: Blackwater fever (haemoglobinuric nephrosis)
options.B: Cerebral malaria
options.C: Splenic rupture

questions.explanation: In falciparum malaria, massive absorption of haemoglobin (released by destroyed red cells) by the renal tubules produces blackwater fever, also called haemoglobinuric nephrosis.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: A postnatal patient reports backache localized specifically over the lumbar region (rather than the sacrum). This location most likely points to:

options.A: Pelvic pathology exclusively
options.B: An orthopedic condition, which is often relieved by physiotherapy
options.C: It always indicates retained products of conception
options.D: It is never a genuine finding after delivery

questions.explanation: Postnatal backache over the sacrum is more likely due to pelvic pathology, while backache over the lumbar region is more likely due to an orthopedic cause, and is often relieved by physiotherapy.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Postnatal Care, Management of Ailments
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: The ulna is often described as the 'stabilising bone' of the forearm because:

options.A: Its trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus, giving the radius a stable foundation from which to pronate and supinate
options.B: It is the only bone that moves during pronation/supination
options.C: It bears the entire weight of the upper limb at the wrist joint
options.D: It has no muscular attachments, unlike the radius

questions.explanation: The ulna's trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus at the elbow, forming a stable hinge. This gives the radius the fixed foundation it needs to rotate around the ulna for efficient pronation and supination of the hand.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The chronic form of filariasis, characterised by lymphoedema and gross thickening of the skin of the legs/scrotum, is known as:

options.A: Elephantiasis
options.B: Cysticercosis
options.C: Amoeboma

questions.explanation: Chronic filariasis (caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi) produces lymphadenopathy, lymphoedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis — enormous thickening and induration of the skin, resembling the hide of an elephant, due to chronic lymphatic obstruction.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Filariasis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Which of the following tumour names is a notable EXCEPTION to standard nomenclature, since despite ending in '-oma' (usually implying benign), it actually refers to a malignant tumour?

options.A: Lipoma
options.B: Fibroma
options.C: Melanoma

questions.explanation: Although the suffix '-oma' generally denotes a benign tumour, several names break this rule: melanoma (malignant tumour of melanocytes), hepatoma (a term sometimes used for hepatocellular carcinoma), lymphoma (malignant tumour of lymphoid tissue), and seminoma (malignant testicular tumour) are all malignant despite the '-oma' ending.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Blastomas (embryomas) such as neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), and retinoblastoma are notable because they:

options.A: Occur almost exclusively in adults over 60
options.B: Arise from embryonal/partially differentiated cells and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5
options.C: Are always benign despite the '-oma' name

questions.explanation: Blastomas arise from embryonal or partially differentiated cells that would normally form the blastema of organs/tissues during embryogenesis, and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology
